title: RabbitMQ vs Kafka, honestly
summary: What each broker is built for in 2026, where they overlap, how to measure instead of guess, and a weighted scoring matrix with knock-out criteria.

steps.title: Smart broker, dumb log
body: | Model | broker routes and tracks every message (exchanges → queues) | append-only partitioned log; consumers track their offsets |
| Routing | direct, topic (`*`, `#`), fanout, headers exchanges; alternate exchanges | topic plus key; anything smarter happens in consumers or Kafka Streams |
| After consume | acked messages are deleted (queues); streams keep them | kept until retention or compaction removes them |
| Replay | streams only (`x-stream-offset`) | any group, any offset or timestamp |
| Per-message features | TTL, dead-letter exchange, quorum-queue delivery limit (default 20), delayed retry via TTL + DLX | none built in: retry and DLQ topics are yours to build |
| Scaling consumers | any number compete on a queue; prefetch bounds each | at most one per partition per group |
| Ordering | per queue (with one active consumer) | per partition |
| Replication | quorum queues (Raft); classic mirrored queues were removed in 4.0 | replication factor + `min.insync.replicas`; KRaft only since 4.0 |
| Throughput shape | each queue has one leader; scale with more queues (or super streams) | scale with partitions and brokers, batching and compression |
Neither is "faster" in the abstract. RabbitMQ is built for per-message work and flexible routing; Kafka for
high-volume, retained, replayable streams with many readers.

steps.prompt: Which broker gives you this out of the box?
items: Dead-letter exchange and a delivery limit on quorum queues
Log compaction: keep the latest value per key
Transactions that commit output records and input offsets together
Replay from an offset or a timestamp
Replicated storage that survives losing a node
steps.explain: Replay is "both" only thanks to RabbitMQ **streams**: a classic or quorum queue cannot replay what was acked.

steps.prompt: Which statements are accurate in 2026? Select all that apply.
options: Quorum queues are RabbitMQ's replicated queue type; classic mirrored queues were removed in RabbitMQ 4.0
Kafka 4.x runs without ZooKeeper: KRaft is the only mode
A quorum queue keeps acked messages so a new consumer can replay them
Confluent.Kafka producers enable idempotence by default, like the Java client
RabbitMQ streams let consumers re-read from an offset or a timestamp
explain: The Java producer defaults to `enable.idempotence=true` since Kafka 3.0; librdkafka (and so Confluent.Kafka) does
not, so set `EnableIdempotence = true` yourself. Quorum queues delete acked messages like any queue.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: measure before you argue
steps.body: Reach for these to load-test a candidate broker with your message size and your durability settings, and to watch it while the test runs.

toolkit.cmd: kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic perf --num-records 1000000 --record-size 1024 --throughput -1 --producer-props bootstrap.servers=kafka:9092 acks=all linger.ms=5 compression.type=lz4
toolkit.what: Records/s and latency percentiles for a Kafka producer.
flags: measure at acks=all, the setting you will actually run
how many to read (recent releases rename it to --num-records; check --help)
against a quorum queue named perf

toolkit.what: Where RabbitMQ's memory goes while the test runs.
Memory and disk alarms, which block publishers.

toolkit.when: For Kafka use JMX or an exporter.

toolkit.what: Disk per partition, for retention sizing.

toolkit.cmd: new ProducerConfig { LingerMs = 5, BatchSize = 1000000, CompressionType = CompressionType.Lz4 }
toolkit.what: Kafka producer settings that move the numbers.
Kafka consumer settings that move the numbers.
flags: the broker waits for at least this much data per fetch
up to 50 unacked messages per consumer
toolkit.when: Pair it with publisher confirms and a bounded number of publishes in flight.

pairs: The durability you will really run

steps.prompt: Generating load, or watching the broker while it runs?
Match each requirement to the better fit and the feature that makes it so.
pairs: Email jobs: retry after 30 s, park after 5 attempts
RabbitMQ: TTL retry queue plus a dead-letter exchange
Clickstream at 500k events/s, kept 7 days, read by three teams
Kafka: partitions scale out, each team is a consumer group
Latest price per SKU, rebuilt by new services at startup

RabbitMQ: a topic exchange with bindings

steps.explain: Notice the last pair: the right answer depends on the team as much as on the feature list.

steps.prompt: A first-pass scoring matrix. What does this print?
code: int Score(Dictionary<string, int> s) => weights.Sum(w => w.Value * s[w.Key]);
explain: Kafka: 15 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 26. RabbitMQ: 6 + 10 + 10 + 3 = 29. A three-point gap on a matrix you made up is not a
decision. The weights are the real argument: write them down and agree on them **before** scoring.

steps.prompt: A RabbitMQ shop wants 7 days of replay. Complete the stream declaration and a consumer that starts from the beginning.
code: await channel.QueueDeclareAsync("orders.stream", durable: true, exclusive: false, autoDelete: false,
await channel.BasicQosAsync(prefetchSize: 0, prefetchCount: 100, global: false);   // streams require a prefetch
await channel.BasicConsumeAsync("orders.stream", autoAck: __2__, consumerTag: "", noLocal: false, exclusive: false,
arguments: new Dictionary<string, object?> { ["x-stream-offset"] = "__3__" }, consumer: consumer);
explain: `x-stream-offset` takes `first`, `last`, `next`, a numeric offset or a timestamp. `earliest` is Kafka's
`auto.offset.reset` vocabulary, not RabbitMQ's. Stream consumers must use manual acks and a prefetch; the acks only
move the credit window, they do not delete anything.

steps.title: A scoring matrix with knock-outs
prompt: Turn the matrix into a function the review can rerun when someone challenges a weight. Write
`List<string> Rank(Dictionary<string, int> weights, Dictionary<string, Dictionary<string, int>> scores, Dictionary<string, int> minimums)`:
- An option's score is the sum over `weights` of `weight * score`; a criterion missing from an option's scores counts as 0.
- **Knock-outs**: an option is excluded when any criterion in `minimums` scores below its minimum (missing = 0).
Report the first failing criterion in alphabetical (ordinal) order.
- Return the ranked options as `"{name} {score}"`, highest score first, ties by name (ordinal); then the excluded
starter: List<string> Rank(Dictionary<string, int> weights, Dictionary<string, Dictionary<string, int>> scores, Dictionary<string, int> minimums)
solution: List<string> Rank(Dictionary<string, int> weights, Dictionary<string, Dictionary<string, int>> scores, Dictionary<string, int> minimums)
var ranked = new List<(string Name, int Score)>();
foreach (var name in scores.Keys.OrderBy(n => n, StringComparer.Ordinal))
hints: Go through the options by name. For each, find the first failing minimum with `minimums.Keys.OrderBy(k => k, StringComparer.Ordinal).FirstOrDefault(...)`.
Sort the survivors with `OrderByDescending(r => r.Score).ThenBy(r => r.Name, StringComparer.Ordinal)`, then append the excluded lines.
template: var dojoScores = new Dictionary<string, Dictionary<string, int>>
Dojo.Eq("weighted ranking with a knock-out", new List<string> { "rabbitmq 37", "kafka 30", "excluded sqs: replay 0 < 2" },
Dojo.Eq("no minimums: everyone is ranked", new List<string> { "rabbitmq 37", "kafka 30", "sqs 24" },
Dojo.Eq("a missing score counts as 0", new List<string> { "b 6", "a 4" },
new Dictionary<string, Dictionary<string, int>> { ["a"] = new() { ["x"] = 2 }, ["b"] = new() { ["y"] = 2 } },
Dojo.Eq("ties are broken by name", new List<string> { "alpha 4", "beta 4" },
new Dictionary<string, Dictionary<string, int>> { ["beta"] = new() { ["x"] = 4 }, ["alpha"] = new() { ["x"] = 4 } },
Dojo.Eq("several failures: the first criterion alphabetically is reported", new List<string> { "excluded kafka: ops 2 < 3", "excluded rabbitmq: replay 2 < 3", "excluded sqs: replay 0 < 3" },
